title: Women of the early Khalsa
hookLine: women took amrit from the start and fought, served, taught and led

cards: A sign-in sheet at a gurdwara, a class list, a wedding card. Read down the names and a pattern shows up. Harpreet Kaur.
Jasleen Kaur. Manjit Kaur. Different first names, the same second one, again and again, where another family's surname might be.

It isn't a family name at all. It's a name given by faith, carried by Sikh women whether their families came from one village or from across the world. Where did it come from, and what was it meant to say?

teach.h: SINGH FOR MEN, KAUR FOR WOMEN.
teach.b: Sikh tradition ties the name to the Khalsa. Men who took amrit were given the name Singh, lion. Women were given Kaur, a name Sikhs explain as princess.

As Sikhs tell it, the effect was the same for both: an old surname that announced caste and clan was set aside, and the Khalsa shared a family name instead. A princess answers to no one's idea of where she belongs.

Tradition places women in this from the start. The tellings of the first amrit put a woman's hand in the bowl, whether they name Mata Jito or Mata Sahib Kaur, whom Sikhs call the mother of the Khalsa.
In the tellings, women took amrit and kept the Khalsa's discipline alongside men. Then look at what they did.

teach.h: THEY FOUGHT, LED, SERVED AND TAUGHT.
teach.b: Some fought: Mai Bhago, whom we met this week, led the deserters back and later served as the Guru's guard. Some led: Mata Sundari, after Guru Gobind Singh, guided the Sikhs through letters and counsel.

Some served and taught, keeping kitchens, raising children in the faith, reciting Gurbani in homes that had no granthi nearby. Sikhs often quote a line of Guru Nanak's here, from Asa di Var in the Guru Granth Sahib.
In paraphrase, it asks why woman should be called lesser, when from her kings are born.
So, as Sikhs explain it, Kaur isn't a decoration but a statement: a woman who signs it signs as royalty, as family, and as a full member of the Khalsa.

how: Sikh women take the name Kaur, as Sikh men take Singh, and the Sikh code of conduct gives it at amrit; Sikhs remember Mata Sahib Kaur, Mai Bhago and Mata Sundari among the women of the early Khalsa.

games.q: the Khalsa is being formed, and the old surnames all announce caste and clan. what should the women of the Khalsa be called?
games.why: Sikh tradition gives women the name Kaur, princess, so that they share a family name in the Khalsa instead of a caste name.

practice: Bring to mind one woman who led you somewhere: a grandmother who held a family together, a teacher who expected more of you, a friend who went first. Name, silently, what she actually did, not just that she was kind.
If she's gone, simply hold her name with honor.
